questions.q: What distinction does this lesson draw between 'can we build a hybrid model' and 'should we build one'?
options: Technical feasibility (demonstrated in Chapter 5's labs) says nothing about whether doing so actually improves a specific project -- that requires a separate, honest justification
There is no real distinction; if something can be built, it should always be built
'Should we' is purely a legal question, unrelated to engineering considerations
The question only applies to classical models, never to quantum ones
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates demonstrated technical capability from the separate, harder question of whether adding a quantum component is a good engineering decision for a specific problem -- which, per Chapter 1's evidence, it almost never is today for production use.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say classical simulation of a quantum circuit becomes extremely expensive beyond roughly 20-30 qubits?
options: A state vector's size grows as 2^n, so simulating 30 qubits requires tracking over a billion complex amplitudes
Classical computers cannot represent complex numbers at all
Simulating more than 20 qubits is mathematically undefined
This limit only applies to amplitude encoding, never to angle encoding
questions.explain: The number of amplitudes in a quantum state vector is 2^n for n qubits, so at 30 qubits that's over a billion amplitudes to track classically -- a real, concrete scaling cost for simulation-based development.

questions.q: In the worked fraud-detection example, which checklist item makes the strongest case AGAINST using a hybrid quantum classifier for that specific production use case?
options: Real-time fraud detection needs low latency, but quantum hardware round-trips add exactly the kind of latency a production system can't tolerate -- combined with no specific mechanism cited for why fraud detection specifically benefits from a quantum component
Fraud detection datasets are too small to ever need a classifier of any kind
Quantum computers cannot process any numeric data, so fraud features can't be encoded at all
There is no valid classical baseline for fraud detection to compare against
questions.explain: The lesson specifically flags the latency cost of quantum hardware round-trips as incompatible with real-time production fraud detection, combined with the vague, non-specific justification ('quantum is good at patterns') failing checklist item 1.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what would need to change to make the fraud-detection scenario a legitimate thing to build, even if not as a production system?
options: Reframe it as a research exploration using a small, barren-plateau-safe feature subset, with an explicit, honestly-accounted comparison against a well-tuned classical baseline
Nothing could ever make this a legitimate project under any framing
Simply using more qubits and a deeper ansatz would resolve all the concerns
Switching from PennyLane to Qiskit Machine Learning would resolve all the concerns
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly describes this reframing -- small scope, barren-plateau-safe design, and a fair classical-baseline comparison -- as exactly the legitimate research structure Chapter 6's project follows, distinct from a production commitment.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a real cost of a hybrid model BEYOND simple runtime slowness?
options: Harder debugging (one more fundamentally different failure-mode-prone component), team/maintenance risk from fewer engineers knowing the stack, and reproducibility issues from hardware calibration drift
Hybrid models are actually cheaper to maintain than any classical model, with zero added costs
Hybrid models eliminate the need for any classical baseline comparison
There are no costs beyond runtime speed; everything else is identical to a classical model
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists debugging difficulty, team/maintenance risk, and reproducibility concerns from hardware calibration drift as real costs distinct from and beyond simple runtime/latency concerns.
